narrative:
The model estimates a 45% chance that you will leave your job. Because this probability is high enough to flag risk, the organization has decided to deny your promotion.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. First, the fact that you have not received other job offers while in your current role actually worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward staying. Most employees predicted to stay also report no external offers, so this is fairly typical. Second, your relatively short overall career experience of only 1-5 years pulled the prediction toward leaving. Half of employees expected to stay have the same limited experience, yet the model still sees shorter tenure as a notable risk factor for turnover. Third, you described getting involved in your job—such as sharing opinions or joining decisions—as difficult. This is uncommon; only 10% of employees predicted to stay feel the same way, and this perception strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to leave.

Taken together, your limited experience and sense that it is hard to participate meaningfully at work outweighed the protective effect of having no outside offers, tipping the balance enough for the system to predict departure.

The organization should consider discussing ways to increase your voice in day-to-day decisions and explore structured support for building broader experience. You may want to reflect on whether clearer pathways for involvement and growth would change how long you see yourself staying.
